version_history.subject: [PATCH] mm: madvise: drop MADV_PAGEOUT folios at swap writeback completion

patches_submitted.patch_summary: This patch improves the handling of MADV_PAGEOUT folios on asynchronous swap devices by marking them as dropbehind at isolation time instead of waiting for writeback completion. This allows the memory to be freed earlier, reducing latency and improving performance. The patch also updates various kernel modules to handle the new behavior correctly.

review_comments.author: David (Arm)
review_comments.summary: Reviewer David (Arm) pointed out that the patch's behavior for MADV_PAGEOUT is inconsistent with synchronous I/O, where memory is released immediately after sync I/O completion. He argued that delaying the release until a later scan may improve swapcache hits before folios are reclaimed, but questioned whether this is relevant in practice and suggested that evicting pages as soon as possible would be more beneficial for freeing up memory.
review_comments.raw_body:
On 9/21/26 17:24, Alexandre Ghiti wrote:
> On an asynchronous swap device MADV_PAGEOUT only marks the folio
> PG_reclaim and rotates it to the tail of the inactive list once its
> writeback completes, so the memory is not actually freed until a later
> reclaim scan removes the by then clean swap cache folio.
But we have the same behavior when just reclaiming memory ordinarily? It's added
to the swapcache and only the next scan actually frees up the memory.

Wouldn't we memory we reclaim ... just gone, like in the sync case?

-- 
Cheers,

David

review_comments.author: Barry Song
review_comments.summary: Barry Song noted that asynchronous swap devices can experience a cold/hot inversion when rotating writeback folios to the tail of the inactive list due to fast NVMe I/O, where some pages complete writeback during isolation while others remain under writeback. He suggested skipping the later scan and reclaiming the folios immediately once the I/O completes for MADV_PAGEOUT, which is an explicit hint from userspace to reclaim memory.

On Mon, Sep 21, 2026 at 11:37 PM David Hildenbrand (Arm)
<david@kernel.org> wrote:
>
> On 9/21/26 17:24, Alexandre Ghiti wrote:
> > On an asynchronous swap device MADV_PAGEOUT only marks the folio
> > PG_reclaim and rotates it to the tail of the inactive list once its
> > writeback completes, so the memory is not actually freed until a later
> > reclaim scan removes the by then clean swap cache folio.
> But we have the same behavior when just reclaiming memory ordinarily? It's added
> to the swapcache and only the next scan actually frees up the memory.
>
> Wouldn't we memory we reclaim ... just gone, like in the sync case?

For synchronous I/O, such as zswap and zram, the memory is released
immediately after sync I/O is done.

For asynchronous I/O, such as NVMe, the swapcache is currently
expected to be rotated back to the tail of the LRU and wait for
another scan. Alexandre once mentioned that when he tried handling
async I/O the same way as sync I/O—releasing the memory once the I/O
completed—he saw some regression. So, delaying the release until a
later scan may allow swapcache hits before the folios are eventually
reclaimed.

But we actually have a problem here: this rotation, which puts
writeback folios at the tail of the LRU, is not reliable at all.

`folio_rotate_reclaimable()` would only work reliably if the endio
happens after the folio has been put back on the LRU head, rather than
while it is still isolated.

But nowadays NVMe is very fast. If we isolate N pages and perform
shrink on them, M pages may finish writeback during the isolation,
while the remaining N-M pages are still under writeback. M can easily
be more than 50% of N.

As a result, we can end up with the following cold/hot inversion:

LRU head
----- M pages whose writeback completed during isolation
----- other pages
----- N-M pages that are successfully rotated to the LRU tail
LRU tail

Now we can see that the M pages were expected to be reclaimed, but
they are not only left unreclaimed, but are effectively promoted to
the LRU head.

For MGLRU, commit 359a5e1416ca ("mm: multi-gen LRU: retry folios
written back while isolated") added the following code to reclaim
those M pages that finish writeback during isolation by retrying
`shrink_folio_list()` on them:

                /* retry folios that may have missed
folio_rotate_reclaimable() */
                if (!skip_retry && !folio_test_active(folio) &&
!folio_mapped(folio) &&
                    !folio_test_dirty(folio) && !folio_test_writeback(folio)) {
                        list_move(&folio->lru, &clean);
                        continue;
                }

This somehow resolves the cold/hot inversion, but leaves the M and
N-M pages with inconsistent behavior: some are actually reclaimed,
while others remain at the tail of the LRU.

For the active/inactive LRU and `MADV_PAGEOUT`, we don't have a
mechanism to restore the missed reclaim opportunity. Ridong's patch[1]
addresses this cold/hot inversion in the active/inactive LRU reclaim
path. To my knowledge, there has never been a patch to address the
same cold/hot inversion in `MADV_PAGEOUT`.

BTW, if `MADV_PAGEOUT` is an explicit hint from userspace to reclaim
the memory, would it make sense to skip the later scan and reclaim the
folios immediately once the I/O completes?

[1] https://lore.kernel.org/linux-mm/20260920132519.3369946-1-ridong.chen@linux.dev/

Best Regards
Barry

> But we actually have a problem here: this rotation, which puts
> writeback folios at the tail of the LRU, is not reliable at all.
>
> `folio_rotate_reclaimable()` would only work reliably if the endio
> happens after the folio has been put back on the LRU head, rather than
> while it is still isolated.

I think we might better fix this instead? Or is this really a problem?
If it has PG_reclaim, it should be putback to the tail instead of
head, right?

> But nowadays NVMe is very fast. If we isolate N pages and perform
> shrink on them, M pages may finish writeback during the isolation,
> while the remaining N-M pages are still under writeback. M can easily
> be more than 50% of N.
>
> As a result, we can end up with the following cold/hot inversion:
>
> LRU head
> ----- M pages whose writeback completed during isolation
> ----- other pages
> ----- N-M pages that are successfully rotated to the LRU tail
> LRU tail
>
> Now we can see that the M pages were expected to be reclaimed, but
> they are not only left unreclaimed, but are effectively promoted to
> the LRU head.
>

> written back while isolated") added the following code to reclaim
> those M pages that finish writeback during isolation by retrying
> `shrink_folio_list()` on them:
>
>                 /* retry folios that may have missed
> folio_rotate_reclaimable() */
>                 if (!skip_retry && !folio_test_active(folio) &&
> !folio_mapped(folio) &&
>                     !folio_test_dirty(folio) && !folio_test_writeback(folio)) {
>                         list_move(&folio->lru, &clean);
>                         continue;
>                 }
>
> This somehow resolves the cold/hot inversion, but leaves the M and
> N-M pages with inconsistent behavior: some are actually reclaimed,
> while others remain at the tail of the LRU.
>
> For the active/inactive LRU and `MADV_PAGEOUT`, we don't have a
> mechanism to restore the missed reclaim opportunity. Ridong's patch[1]
> addresses this cold/hot inversion in the active/inactive LRU reclaim
> path. To my knowledge, there has never been a patch to address the
> same cold/hot inversion in `MADV_PAGEOUT`.

MADV_PAGEOUT is a bit different from the reclaim under pressure,
reclaim underpressure can easily overshoot the amount of anon folios
reclaimed, because however fast the writeback it, it can be faster by
scanning the LRU and dropping clean file folios. So before LRU
reclaimed enough clean file folios, we can't stop the reclaim.

I think the better fix is to have a separate watermark for anon / file
or a new way to handle reclaim. Reclaiming an anon folio is hardly
helpful in the short term when under heavy pressure and the device is
not a synchronous device.

The overshoot is a real issue, it's very common to see many folios
stuck in the swap cache after memory pressure. If we drop all of them,
we will see significant regressions. Treating MADV_PAGEOUT differently
here seems better.

This approach allows the system to recover unallocated space and improves the chances of successfully allocating system chunks. The original code combined page-table iteration with validation and processing in a single loop, which made it difficult to understand the batching rules for large folios and the ownership transferred when a partial folio is split. By moving this logic into a separate function, the patch improves the clarity and maintainability of the code without introducing any functional changes.

series_items.subject: [PATCH 08/10] mm/madvise: separate the PTL-held PTE scan
series_items.patch_summary: This patch separates the PTE scan in the madvise function from its surrounding lock drops, allowing it to run entirely under the PTE lock. The scan is moved into a helper function that returns a locked and referenced split candidate or stops at the existing scheduling boundary. This change does not introduce any functional changes but improves the code's structure and efficiency.

series_items.subject: [PATCH 09/10] mm/madvise: make cold and pageout PTE lock ownership explicit
series_items.patch_summary: This patch refactors the madvise_lru_pte_range_locked function to explicitly manage PTE lock ownership, making it clear who holds the lock during page-walking and huge PMD handling. The original code mixed lock ownership between the PMD callback and the page-walk callback, which is now separated into two distinct functions. This change does not introduce any functional changes but improves the clarity of the code by explicitly managing lock ownership.

series_items.subject: [PATCH 10/10] mm/madvise: share cold and pageout walk setup
series_items.patch_summary: This patch refactors the shared TLB and page-walk setup for MADV_COLD and MADV_PAGEOUT operations in the Linux kernel's mm/madvise module. It introduces a new helper function, madvise_lru_vma_range(), which is used by both entry points to perform the common setup tasks. The patch aims to reduce code duplication and improve maintainability without introducing any functional changes.

patches_submitted.patch_summary: This patch series refactors the cold and pageout page table walks in the Linux kernel's mm/madvise module to improve code readability, maintainability, and performance. The current implementation is a complex nest of functions that handle various scenarios, including huge PMDs, PTE-mapped large folios, ordinary PTEs, folio splitting, and deferred PAGEOUT reclaim. The series separates these responsibilities into distinct functions, making the code easier to understand and audit.

series_items.subject: [PATCH v3 1/7] mm: support promotion-only NUMA hinting scans
series_items.patch_summary: This patch introduces a new NUMA hinting scan mode called 'promotion-only' that allows the kernel to identify when a VMA becomes active, without applying heuristics like read-only VMAs or activeness. The patch adds a new flag MM_CP_PROT_NUMA_PROMO_ONLY and modifies task_numa_work() to select the type of walk based on this flag. It also updates folio_can_map_prot_numa() to derive the single-threaded private state at the point of use, rather than adding another precomputed boolean to the protection-walk interface. This change is required for memory-tiering fixes and must be accompanied by them when backported.

series_items.subject: [PATCH v3 2/7] mm: allow shared folios to be promoted to a fast tier
series_items.patch_summary: This patch allows shared copy-on-write folios and executable file folios mapped by multiple processes to be promoted from slow memory to a faster tier, but only in specific migration scenarios where the destination is top-tier (south->north). The existing restrictions for ordinary placement and non-promotion migrations remain intact. Additionally, the function name `folio_use_access_time` has been renamed to `folio_in_lowtier` to make its condition more obvious.

series_items.subject: [PATCH v3 3/7] sched/numa: scan read-only file mappings in tiering mode
series_items.patch_summary: This patch modifies the NUMA balancing code to scan read-only file mappings when tiering is enabled, but only for promotion purposes. It keeps the existing restriction on excluding shared libraries from migration. The change allows hot files to be promoted to faster memory tiers, improving performance in certain workloads.

series_items.subject: [PATCH v3 4/7] sched/numa: separate VMA placement from scan continuation
series_items.patch_summary: This patch separates the decision to place a VMA (Virtual Memory Area) for east-west sampling from the continuation of an ongoing scan across multiple scan windows. The helper function vma_is_accessed() is renamed to vma_needs_placement_scan() and its logic is split between determining placement eligibility and handling scan progress. This change allows PID-inactive VMAs to be scanned without mistakenly treating scan continuation as evidence of placement eligibility, which is a prerequisite for the next fix in this series.

series_items.subject: [PATCH v3 5/7] sched/numa: scan PID-inactive VMAs for promotion
series_items.patch_summary: This patch modifies the Linux kernel's NUMA (Non-Uniform Memory Access) memory management to scan VMAs (Virtual Memory Areas) that are not currently active due to lack of recent PID activity. This allows for promotion-only scans, which update the VMA's previous scan sequence but do not advance the placement-starvation horizon. The patch also introduces a new field in the vma_numab_state structure to track the last completed placement scan separately from other scans. This change is intended to improve memory tiering and reduce CXL bandwidth utilization on hosts with large amounts of DRAM and CXL memory.

series_items.subject: [PATCH v3 6/7] mm: use BIT() for change_protection() flags
series_items.patch_summary: This patch updates the MM_CP_* flags in include/linux/mm.h to use the BIT() macro consistently, replacing open-coded shifts. This change does not introduce any functional changes and is intended to improve code readability and maintainability.

series_items.subject: [PATCH v3 7/7] mm: use VMA flag helpers in NUMA balancing
series_items.patch_summary: This patch updates the NUMA balancing code in the Linux kernel to use VMA flag helpers instead of directly accessing vm_flags. The changes are made in three files: kernel/sched/fair.c, mm/internal.h, and mm/migrate.c. The patch does not introduce any functional changes but rather simplifies the code by using the vma_test() function to check for specific flags. This change is intended to make the code more maintainable and easier to understand.

patches_submitted.patch_summary: This patch series addresses poor NUMA balancing behavior in a production deployment by modifying the VMA scan filters to no longer gate memory-tier promotion. The issue arises from the global balancing mode being unable to describe the intent of individual VMA/PTE walks (placement vs promotion). The patches introduce promotion-only NUMA protection walks, derive private VMA state for eligibility checks, and separate VMA placement eligibility from partial-scan continuation. This allows eligible shared folios to be promoted to a fast tier and improves overall system performance by increasing DRAM bandwidth and reducing request latency.

series_items.subject: [PATCH v2 1/8] nfsd: clear NFSD_NET_UP before dropping the generic resource reference
series_items.patch_summary: This patch fixes a potential issue in the NFS daemon where the NFSD_NET_UP flag is left set after shutting down the generic resources, causing inconsistencies when accessing host-wide file cache and NFSv4 tables. The patch clears the NFSD_NET_UP flag before dropping the reference to the generic resources, ensuring that the invariant 'NFSD_NET_UP implies the generic resources are up' holds true. This change has no functional impact on the system's behavior.

series_items.subject: [PATCH v2 2/8] nfsd: make max_blksize a per-namespace setting
series_items.patch_summary: This patch makes the maximum block size a per-namespace setting in the NFS daemon, rather than a global module-scope variable. This change prevents containerized environments from affecting other namespaces' payload sizes. The patch moves the max_blksize field into the struct nfsd_net and updates various functions to use this new field instead of the global variable. As a result, each namespace can now have its own maximum block size, which is set lazily on first server start in that namespace.

series_items.subject: [PATCH v2 3/8] nfsd: move the control plane to a per-namespace mutex
series_items.patch_summary: This patch moves the control plane of the NFS daemon (nfsd) to a per-namespace mutex, allowing for concurrent operations across different network namespaces. The global nfsd_mutex is retained only for host-wide serialization, such as user refcounts and resource management. The change improves performance by reducing contention between namespaces and allows for more efficient handling of dynamic-thread autoscaling and RPC_STATUS_GET dumps.

series_items.subject: [PATCH v2 4/8] nfsd: rename nfsd_mutex to nfsd_global_mutex
series_items.patch_summary: This patch renames the 'nfsd_mutex' to 'nfsd_global_mutex' in various NFS daemon files, providing clarity on which mutex is being referenced at each call site. This change does not introduce any functional changes but rather improves code readability and maintainability. The rename affects several files within the NFS daemon's source code, including filecache.c, netns.h, nfsctl.c, nfsd.h, and nfssvc.c.

series_items.subject: [PATCH v2 5/8] nfsd: give the open file cache its own mutex
series_items.patch_summary: This patch introduces a new mutex, nfsd_file_cache_mutex, to protect the open file cache in the NFS server. The global mutex, nfsd_global_mutex, is no longer used for file cache operations, which were previously serialized against server start/stop. The new mutex is held by the file cache initialization and shutdown functions, as well as by readers and walkers that need access to the cache. This change improves concurrency and reduces contention between unrelated namespaces.

series_items.subject: [PATCH v2 6/8] selftests/nfsd: factor the netlink plumbing into a shared header
series_items.patch_summary: This patch extracts the netlink plumbing code from nfsd_netlink_listener.c into a shared header file, nfsd_netlink.h. The shared header contains static inline functions that handle generic-netlink client setup, attribute packing, extack parsing, and family resolution. This allows other NFS selftests to reuse this common functionality without having to duplicate the code or link against it.

series_items.subject: [PATCH v2 7/8] selftests/nfsd: add cross-namespace isolation tests
series_items.patch_summary: This patch adds a new selftest to the NFS daemon (nfsd) that checks for cross-namespace isolation. The test creates multiple namespaces, each with its own nfsd server and filesystem, and verifies that changes made in one namespace do not affect others. It tests various settings and behaviors, including NFSD settings, running servers, and listener management, to ensure they are properly isolated between namespaces.

series_items.subject: [PATCH v2 8/8] selftests/nfsd: add a cross-namespace control-plane soak
series_items.patch_summary: This patch adds a self-test to the NFS daemon (NFSD) that exercises its control plane from multiple namespaces simultaneously, testing lock nesting and serialization between namespaces. The test runs for a specified amount of time, during which each namespace churns through various operations, including starting and stopping servers, emptying listener sets, and reading file caches. The test also checks for lockdep splats and refcount saturation, and reports any failures or warnings. The patch includes configuration options to control the number of namespaces and the duration of the test.

series_items.subject: [PATCH v2 1/3] mm/huge_memory: make thp_underused() work for mTHP folios
series_items.patch_summary: This patch modifies the thp_underused() function to make it work with mTHP folios, which are larger than PMD-sized folios. The function is made size-aware instead of hardcoded to PMD-sized folios. A new helper function, thp_can_be_underused(), is introduced to check if a folio can be underused based on the number of zero-filled pages and the sysctl maximum value. This change will allow anonymous mTHP folios to be added to the deferred split list in future patches.

series_items.subject: [PATCH v2 2/3] mm/huge_memory: don't queue folios that can never be underused
series_items.patch_summary: This patch optimizes the handling of anonymous PMD-sized folios in the Linux kernel by skipping the queuing of folios that can never be underused, reducing unnecessary work and improving performance. The default khugepaged/max_ptes_none setting causes the shrinker to never split these folios for being underused, so they are not queued. This change is particularly important for a subsequent patch that adds anonymous mTHP folios to the deferred split list, as it prevents small mTHP orders from taking the list_lru lock on every anonymous fault.

series_items.subject: [PATCH v2 3/3] mm/memory: add anonymous mTHP folios to the deferred split list
series_items.patch_summary: This patch adds anonymous mTHP (huge page) folios to the deferred split list in the Linux kernel's memory management code. This allows for underused splitting of huge pages, which can help reclaim unused parts of large memory allocations when the system is under memory pressure. The patch addresses a problem where fully mapped huge pages that are mostly zero-filled do not get split by the deferred split shrinker, leading to memory regressions. The solution involves mirroring the behavior for PMD-sized folios and adding a check to minimize overhead on common fault paths.

patches_submitted.patch_summary: This patch series addresses memory regressions caused by enabling 2M THP=always on arm64 with 64k base pages. The patches split underused anonymous mTHP folios, which are not currently reclaimed under memory pressure. Patch 1 makes the thp_underused() function size-aware to accommodate larger folio sizes. Patch 2 optimizes existing behavior by keeping folios that can never be found underused off the deferred split queue. Patch 3 queues anonymous mTHP folios from map_anon_folio_pte_nopf(), mirroring what is already done for PMD folios. The patches aim to provide a solution for deploying 2M THP=always on arm64 without causing memory regressions.

Some of it can be had in:

commit 5a9c05d86683db5449b7fefd278c461cffb55234
Author: Nico Pache <nico.pache@linux.dev>
Date:   Fri Jun 5 10:14:11 2026 -0600

    mm/khugepaged: generalize __collapse_huge_page_* for mTHP support

    generalize the order of the __collapse_huge_page_* and collapse_max_*
    functions to support future mTHP collapse.

    The current mechanism for determining collapse with the
    khugepaged_max_ptes_none value is not designed with mTHP in mind.  This
    raises a key design issue: if we support user defined max_pte_none values
    (even those scaled by order), a collapse of a lower order can introduces
    an feedback loop, or "creep", when max_ptes_none is set to a value greater
    than HPAGE_PMD_NR / 2.  [1]

    With this configuration, a successful collapse to order N will populate
    enough pages to satisfy the collapse condition on order N+1 on the next
    scan.  This leads to unnecessary work and memory churn.

    To fix this issue introduce a helper function that will limit mTHP
    collapse support to two max_ptes_none values, 0 and HPAGE_PMD_NR - 1.
    This effectively supports two modes: [2]

    - max_ptes_none=0: never collapses if it encounters an empty PTE or a PTE
      that maps the shared zeropage. Consequently, no memory bloat.
    - max_ptes_none=511 (on 4k pagesz): Always collapse to the highest
      available mTHP order.

    This removes the possibility of "creep", and a warning will be emitted if
    any non-supported max_ptes_none value is configured with mTHP enabled.
    Any intermediate value will default mTHP collapse to max_ptes_none=0.

    mTHP collapse will not honor the khugepaged_max_ptes_shared or
    khugepaged_max_ptes_swap parameters, and will fail if it encounters a
    shared or swapped entry.


Tracing back the discussion on that patch should give you all the details.

With scaling, I don't see a way of avoiding having to queue every
anonymous folio of order >=2 to the deferred split list at fault time
in the non-default max_ptes_none case, since any folio can now
potentially qualify as underused. This drew some objections in v1,

out scaling. The objections were a) the list_lru lock contention and
b) the limited upside vs cost of splitting small folios.

problem. If it would be helpful to have some benchmark numbers, I'm
happy to run a synthetic one (patch 3 applied (which adds anon mTHP
folios to the deferred split list), only order-2 enabled,
max_ptes_none set low enough, all threads in one cgroup on one node so
they contend on the same lock, each thread faulting in a large private
anonymous mapping). I'm happy to run something else if anyone has a
workload they would trust more. Johannes also mentioned batching as a
mitigation. If the contention does turn out to be an issue, I'm happy

patches_submitted.subject: [PATCH 2/2] mm: page_alloc: remove ALLOC_NON_BLOCK from ALLOC_RESERVES

version_history.subject: [PATCH 2/2] mm: page_alloc: remove ALLOC_NON_BLOCK from ALLOC_RESERVES

patches_submitted.patch_summary: This patch removes the ALLOC_NON_BLOCK flag from the ALLOC_RESERVES definition in the Linux kernel's page allocation code. The flag was previously used to grant access to a reserve of memory below the minimum watermark, but this caused issues when GFP_NOWAIT allocations were made under memory pressure. By removing the flag, the patch prevents direct reclaim and stalls during such bursts, ensuring that high-order atomic allocations are not disrupted by GFP_NOWAIT consumers. The patch also updates comments in the code to reflect the correct behavior of ALLOC_NON_BLOCK.

This change aims to prevent squandering of reserves on requests that don't need it, improving the overall performance of highatomic requests.
